newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish army warning weighs heavily on shares.
newsitem.headline: Turkish army warning weighs heavily on shares.

text.p: Turkish shares tumbled in nervous trade on Monday after a warning by the army against ruling Islamists sowed fresh market uncertainty about the political situation, analysts and brokers said.
The IMKB National-100 index fell 5.58 percent, or 90 points, to end the day at 1,522. Trading volume soared to 23.14 trillion lira ($188.1 million) from 16.78 trillion on Friday.

Turkey's generals warned the Islamist-led government of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan at Friday's National Security Council (MGK) meeting that they wanted a crackdown on what they saw as a wave of religious zeal threatening secular democracy.
"The decisions of the MGK meeting created uncertainty. These are good opportunities for selling," said Mustafa Karaahmetoglu of Sayilgan Securities.

Market participants said caution ahead of Tuesday's release of February inflation data and a censure motion debate against the government added momentum to the downtrend which accelerated in the afternoon.

Broker Mustafa Yilmaz said market insecurity was reflected in rising volume in the overnight repo market. "An easing in political tension is needed. Newspapers full of pictures of army generals negatively affect the market," he said.
One dealer said a major wave of selling was unleashed by the breaking of an important index support level at 1,580.
Istanbul shares have rallied strongly since the start of the year on hopes for privatisation, jumping 65 percent in lira terms in the last two months.
Official forecasts of $5 billion privatisation revenues and a court go-ahead for the sale of the state telecommunications company Turk Telekom have helped fuel market optimism.
However, anxieties in financial circles about Erbakan's ultimate political aims have been stoked by the military warning and bankers were waiting to see how the Islamist leader would react to it.
"If Erbakan goes on with his old radical declarations it is a danger and the military will escalate the problem," said Oner Ayan, responsible for international capital markets at ATA Securities.
He said the main pressure on Erbakan was likely to come from parliament rather than the military and this would pressure him to backtrack.
"This will increase stability, remove irritants for foreign investors...and attract more foreign capital investment," Ayan said.

He forecast the current political uncertainty, exacerbated by the media, would fade in the coming weeks but the government would remain burdened with long-term challenges of reforming taxation and the social security system.

Despite bold revenue-raising forecasts, the drafting of a balanced budget for 1997 and declining interest rates, the government is still struggling to find a solution to annual inflation running at 85 percent.

The latest price data for February was due out on Tuesday and is expected to show continued strong inflation. Analysts forecast a 4.5-5.5 percent month-on-month rise in consumer prices. Bankers expect bond yields, mixed at around 95-96 percent on Monday, to go up if the monthly price indices came out above 5.5 percent.
The lira eased to 122,900 against the dollar from Friday's close of 122,410.
